name: Psychedelic therapy for self-image

card.summary: Experimental idea of using psychedelics for body image; no direct studies, and the drugs are controlled substances.
card.note: Schedule I in the US; contraindicated with some medications and psychiatric histories.

quick.overview:
Psychedelic therapy uses drugs like psilocybin with guided sessions to treat mental health conditions. Using it for self-image is experimental.

No studies directly examine self-image outcomes.
quick.mechanism: Mechanisms are poorly understood; outcomes depend heavily on mindset and setting.
quick.risks: The drugs are Schedule I in the US. Contraindications include psychosis history, pregnancy and SSRI use.

lead: Psychedelic therapy for self-image is the idea that psychedelic-assisted treatment with substances such as psilocybin, LSD or MDMA could change how a person perceives and feels about their own body and appearance. Interest comes from people with appearance-related distress, including body dysmorphic disorder (BDD), who seek a shift in self-perception so they can feel at ease with how they look rather than changing their looks themselves.[1][2]

Psychedelic therapy more broadly is the use of these drugs in mental health treatment, usually with preparation and integration sessions, and research has concentrated on depression, PTSD, anxiety and substance use.[1] Wikipedia describes psilocybin at high doses as producing ego dissolution, with decreased connectivity in the default mode network, a system tied to introspection and sense of self.[3] A 2024 review noted that a single psilocybin dose given for obsessive-compulsive symptoms raised insight in patients who also had BDD, leading them to seek treatment.[1]

A PubMed search for psilocybin and BDD lists a small body of work, including a 2023 pilot study of single-dose psilocybin in serotonin-reuptake-inhibitor-resistant BDD, a 2025 study of resting-state brain networks after a single dose in BDD patients, a 1996 case report, and a 2020 review of psychedelics and the aberrant bodily self.[5] Psychedelics remain Schedule I in the US and are generally limited to clinical trials.

chain: Psychedelic-assisted sessions alter self-referential brain networks
Possible shift in how one's own appearance is perceived
Less distress about looks (investigated in BDD)
angle.text: The appearance goal is perceptual rather than physical: the aim is for a person to relate to their reflection and body differently, which small early studies in body dysmorphic disorder have begun to examine.

infobox: Schedule I (US); trials or limited programs elsewhere[3]

paras: Wikipedia describes BDD as involving extreme misperceptions of one's appearance, commonly of the face, skin or body, with a muscle dysmorphia subtype in which people see their bodies as too small. Established treatments are SSRIs and cognitive-behavioural therapy, and it notes that cosmetic surgery often does not relieve BDD symptoms.[4]

A 2024 meta-analysis of psilocybin trials found antidepressant effects above placebo, and an FDA panel in 2024 voted against approving MDMA for PTSD.[1] Limitations include small samples, short follow-up and blinding problems.[1] Wikipedia notes psilocybin was approved in Australia for treatment-resistant depression in 2023 and that single doses with psychological support may produce rapid antidepressant effects, with an advantage over continuous SSRI use that may be modest or absent.[3]

For BDD specifically, the available literature identified in PubMed includes a 2023 pilot study of single-dose psilocybin for SRI-resistant BDD and a 2025 imaging study of single-dose effects on resting-state networks.[5]

Contraindications include pregnancy, serious cardiovascular disease, SSRI or MAOI use, and a personal or family history of psychosis or bipolar I disorder.[1] Wikipedia lists panic reactions as common, hallucinogen-induced psychotic disorder as rare (under 1 percent of users), and notes psilocybin is Schedule I under the 1971 UN Convention, with possession of psilocybin mushrooms illegal in most countries.[3]

Small studies in body dysmorphic disorder exist, including a 2023 pilot trial and a 2025 imaging study; no studies have examined psychedelics for everyday looks-related self-image outside that diagnosis.[5] A 2024 review noted increased insight in OCD patients with body dysmorphic disorder after psilocybin.[1]

timeline.event: Case report on serotonin, psilocybin and body dysmorphic disorder published.[5]
Pilot study of single-dose psilocybin in SRI-resistant BDD published.[5]
